The main algorithm uses MM. This section gives two alternatives for the same
fixed-residual scale problem: direct scalar minimization and joint-proximal
splitting. All three use the same coefficient updates and require the same
joint optimality checks after fitting.

For fixed residuals, we write
$$
 f_r(\sigma)=\frac1n\sum_i\sigma h_\rho(r_i/\sigma)+a\sigma,
 \qquad f_r(0)=\frac\rho n\|r\|_1.
$$
If $M=\|r\|_\infty>0$, we set $q=r/M$ and $t=\sigma/M$.
Then $f_r(Mt)=M f_q(t)$, so normalization changes neither the minimizing
scale nor the sign of an objective difference. We write $m=\#\{i:q_i\ne0\}$.
If $M=0$ or $2na\ge m\rho^2$, zero is a scale-block minimizer. Equality
can give a nonunique interval of minimizing scales, and we choose zero.
This block conclusion does not certify the regression coefficients.

For $t>0$,
$$
 D_q(t)=f_q'(t)=a-\frac1{2n}\sum_i
              \min\{q_i^2/t^2,\rho^2\},\qquad
 D_q(0+)=a-\frac{m\rho^2}{2n}.
$$
The derivative is nondecreasing. We define the block stationarity residual
$$
 E_q(t)=\begin{cases}|D_q(t)|,&t>0,\\[-2pt]
                     (-D_q(0+))_+,&t=0.\end{cases}
$$
We also use a dual certificate. We set $w_i=\psi_\rho(q_i/t)$ for $t>0$
and $w_i=\rho\mathrm{sign}(q_i)$ for $t=0$, and define
$$
 \theta=\min\{1,\sqrt{2na}/\|w\|_2\},\quad v=\theta w,
 \qquad
 \Delta_q(t)=\frac{f_q(t)-q^\top v/n}{\max\{1,f_q(t)\}}.
$$
For $w=0$, we take $\theta=1$. Since $\|v\|_\infty\le\rho$ and
$\|v\|_2^2\le2na$, the numerator is a valid primal--dual gap for the
fixed-residual scale problem. In floating point its negative roundoff is
replaced by zero. We write $C_q(t)=\max\{E_q(t),\Delta_q(t)\}$.
An exact or proximal block return is numerically certified when
$C_q(t)\le\epsilon_\sigma$. A finite MM batch need not satisfy this
condition. Joint convergence still requires the coefficient and scale
conditions in the main text.

**Option A: MM.** The MM subroutine below takes at most $B$ MM steps. Each step
minimizes the tangent majorizer derived above. A finite batch is a descent
update, not exact minimization of $f_q$.

**Option B: scalar root.** The scalar-root subroutine solves $D_q(t)=0$ by bisection,
using the bracket
$$
 0\le t_*\le\frac{\|q\|_2}{\sqrt{2na}}.
$$
The previous scale tightens this bracket. This option minimizes the
original scalar block to its declared certificate tolerance. The software name
`exact` denotes scalar minimization to numerical tolerance. Equivalently,
on a consistent inlier set $I=\{i:|q_i|\le\rho t_*\}$,
$$
 t_*^2=\frac{\sum_{i\in I}q_i^2}{2na-(n-|I|)\rho^2},
$$
when the denominator is positive. The implementation uses the monotone
root equation and does not assume that $I$ is known.

**Option C: local joint prox and consensus.** We define the closed perspective
$\phi(u,s)=s h_\rho(u/s)+as$, and
$$
 \mathcal S_q=\{(u,s):u=q,\ s=t\mathbf1\},\qquad
 P_{\mathcal S_q}(u,s)=(q,\bar s\mathbf1).
$$
The lifted problem is
$$
 \min_{u,s}\ \sum_i\phi(u_i,s_i)+\iota_{\mathcal S_q}(u,s).
$$
Its objective on $\mathcal S_q$ is $n f_q(t)$. Thus multiplying the
averaged scale objective by $n$ makes each local proximal term
$\phi$, with step size $\gamma$. No additional factor $1/n$ is applied
inside these proxs. The scale coefficient $a$ appears once per local
term, producing the required $na t$ in the unaveraged objective.

The splitting subroutine applies Douglas--Rachford splitting to this sum and affine
constraint. With $\Phi(u,s)=\sum_i\phi(u_i,s_i)$, its updates are
$$
 p^{(k)}=\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma\Phi}(z^{(k)}),\qquad
 z^{(k+1)}=z^{(k)}+P_{\mathcal S_q}(2p^{(k)}-z^{(k)})-p^{(k)}.
$$
The local operation is the joint perspective prox of
@combettes2020 [Example 2.5], specialized to the present normalization.
For $x=u/\gamma$ and $z=s/\gamma$, we define
$$
 v(\mu)=\mathrm{sign}(x)
       \min\{|x|/(1+\mu),\rho\},\qquad
 H(\mu)=z-\mu+\tfrac12v(\mu)^2-a.
$$
If $H(0)\le0$, we take $\mu=0$. Otherwise $H$ has a unique positive root.
The local prox is
$$
 \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma\phi}(u,s)
       =(u-\gamma v(\mu),\gamma\mu).
$$
The local-prox subroutine evaluates this prox by a scalar root with interval tolerance
$\epsilon_\mu\max\{1,\mu\}$ and at most $K_\mu$ iterations. It handles negative
splitting-scale inputs and the zero-scale output without a scale floor.
The projected feasible point has scale $\bar p_s\ge0$, while its residuals
are fixed at $q$. Splitting iterations need not decrease $f_q$ monotonically.
We therefore retain the best feasible point with objective no larger than
$f_q(t^{(0)})$. A truncated proximal solve can supply a descent step, but is
not reported as an exact block solve unless its certificate passes.

A proposed update is rejected if it increases the original block objective.
The controls $B,\epsilon_\sigma,T,\gamma,K_\mu,\epsilon_\mu$ are listed
in Supplement S1. A finite MM batch or truncated splitting solve may provide
a descent step without minimizing the scale block to tolerance. Fixed-scale
fitting bypasses these operations. The comparison below disables support
Newton steps equally for all three methods.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

~~~{=latex}
\begin{algorithm}[H]
\small\setstretch{1}\DontPrintSemicolon
\caption{\addition{$\mathrm{ScaleMM}(q,t^{(0)};B,\epsilon_\sigma)$}}
\KwInput{$q\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\},\ t^{(0)}>0;\quad \rho,a,\epsilon_\sigma>0,\ B\in\mathbb N_+,\ 2na<\rho^2\#\{i:q_i\ne0\}$}
\KwOutput{$(t,b,\nu)\in[0,\infty)\times\mathbb N_0\times\{0,1\}$}
\addition{
$t\leftarrow t^{(0)}$; $b\leftarrow0$\;
\While{$b<B\ \mathrm{and}\ C_q(t)>\epsilon_\sigma$}{
 $t\leftarrow\{(2an)^{-1}\sum_i\min(q_i^2,\rho^2t^2)\}^{1/2}$; $b\leftarrow b+1$\;
}
\If{$f_q(t)>f_q(t^{(0)})$}{$t\leftarrow t^{(0)}$}
\KwReturn{$(t,b,\mathbf1_{\{C_q(t)\le\epsilon_\sigma\}})$}
}
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[H]
\small\setstretch{1}\DontPrintSemicolon
\caption{\addition{$\mathrm{ScaleRoot}(q,t^{(0)};T,\epsilon_\sigma)$}}
\KwInput{$q\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\},\ t^{(0)}\ge0;\quad \rho,a,\epsilon_\sigma>0,\ T\in\mathbb N_+,\ 2na<\rho^2\#\{i:q_i\ne0\}$}
\KwOutput{$(t,b,\nu)\in[0,\infty)\times\mathbb N_0\times\{0,1\}$}
\addition{
\If{$C_q(t^{(0)})\le\epsilon_\sigma$}{\KwReturn{$(t^{(0)},0,1)$}}
$\ell\leftarrow0$; $h\leftarrow\|q\|_2/\sqrt{2na}$\;
\eIf{$D_q(t^{(0)})<0$}{$\ell\leftarrow t^{(0)}$}{$h\leftarrow\min(h,t^{(0)})$}
\For{$b=1,\ldots,T$}{
 $t\leftarrow(\ell+h)/2$\;
 \If{$C_q(t)\le\epsilon_\sigma$}{\textbf{break}}
 \eIf{$D_q(t)<0$}{$\ell\leftarrow t$}{$h\leftarrow t$}
}
\If{$f_q(t)>f_q(t^{(0)})$}{$t\leftarrow t^{(0)}$}
\KwReturn{$(t,b,\mathbf1_{\{C_q(t)\le\epsilon_\sigma\}})$}
}
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[H]
\small\setstretch{1}\DontPrintSemicolon
\caption{\addition{$\mathrm{ScaleProx}(q,t^{(0)};T,\epsilon_\sigma,\gamma)$}}
\KwInput{$q\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\},\ t^{(0)}\ge0;\quad \rho,a,\epsilon_\sigma>0,\ T\in\mathbb N_+,\ 2na<\rho^2\#\{i:q_i\ne0\}$}
\KwInput{$\gamma>0$}
\KwOutput{$(t,b,\nu)\in[0,\infty)\times\mathbb N_0\times\{0,1\}$}
\addition{
\If{$C_q(t^{(0)})\le\epsilon_\sigma$}{\KwReturn{$(t^{(0)},0,1)$}}
$z_u\leftarrow q$; $z_s\leftarrow t^{(0)}\mathbf1$; $t_*\leftarrow t^{(0)}$\;
\For{$b=1,\ldots,T$}{
 \For{$i=1,\ldots,n$}{$(p_{u,i},p_{s,i})\leftarrow\mathrm{JointProx}(z_{u,i},z_{s,i};\gamma,K_\mu,\epsilon_\mu)$}
 $t\leftarrow n^{-1}\sum_i p_{s,i}$\;
 \If{$f_q(t)<f_q(t_*)$}{$t_*\leftarrow t$}
 \If{$C_q(t)\le\epsilon_\sigma\ \mathrm{and}\ f_q(t)\le f_q(t^{(0)})$}{\KwReturn{$(t,b,1)$}}
 $c\leftarrow n^{-1}\sum_i(2p_{s,i}-z_{s,i})$\;
 $z_u\leftarrow z_u+q-p_u$; $z_s\leftarrow z_s+c\mathbf1-p_s$\;
}
\KwReturn{$(t_*,T,\mathbf1_{\{C_q(t_*)\le\epsilon_\sigma\}})$}
}
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[H]
\small\setstretch{1}\DontPrintSemicolon
\caption{\addition{$\mathrm{JointProx}(u,s;\gamma,K_\mu,\epsilon_\mu)$}}
\KwInput{$u,s\in\mathbb R;\quad \gamma,\rho,a,\epsilon_\mu>0,\ K_\mu\in\mathbb N_+$}
\KwOutput{$\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma\phi}(u,s)$}
\addition{
$x\leftarrow u/\gamma$; $z\leftarrow s/\gamma$;
$v(\mu)\leftarrow\mathrm{sign}(x)\min\{|x|/(1+\mu),\rho\}$\;
$H(\mu)\leftarrow z-\mu+v(\mu)^2/2-a$\;
\If{$H(0)\le0$}{\KwReturn{$(u-\gamma v(0),0)$}}
$\ell\leftarrow0$; $h\leftarrow H(0)$\;
\For{$j=1,\ldots,K_\mu$}{
 $\mu\leftarrow(\ell+h)/2$\;
 \eIf{$H(\mu)>0$}{$\ell\leftarrow\mu$}{$h\leftarrow\mu$}
 \If{$h-\ell\le\epsilon_\mu\max\{1,\mu\}$}{\textbf{break}}
}
$\mu\leftarrow(\ell+h)/2$\;
\KwReturn{$(u-\gamma v(\mu),\gamma\mu)$}
}
\end{algorithm}
~~~

:::

## Numerical comparisons {.unnumbered}

The software exposes `FastHuberCD(scale_update="mm")`, `"exact"`, and
`"prox"`, together with the fixed-residual `update_scale` function.
The comparison below uses three declared $n=45,p=8$ fixtures and three
timing repeats per method, with common starts, penalty, coefficient kernel,
outer tolerance and inner certificate tolerance. Independent reference fits
use the original solver at $\epsilon_{\rm ref}$. Each compared return is
externally checked at $\epsilon_{\rm pilot}$ and relative objective
difference $\epsilon_{\rm obj}$.
Compilation and reference fitting are outside the reported fit times.

{{< include ../analysis/outputs/scale-strategies/results.qmd >}}

: Preliminary implementation validation of the three scale options. Inner iteration counts are method-specific work counts, not equivalent operations. {#tbl-scale-strategies}

All 27 calls pass these checks. On these small fixtures, MM and direct scalar
minimization take similar total fit times, whereas joint-proximal splitting
requires more work. These cases verify the implementations. They do not
establish a general ordering of the methods.

A separate paired path study uses all four ROME designs, sizes $(100,100)$,
$(100,500)$ and $(500,500)$, three seeds per design/size, and 30 common absolute
penalties from the fixed-scale maximum toward 0.05 of that maximum. The
coefficient routines, support steps and accuracy checks are identical for MM
and scalar-root fitting. MM certifies 35/36 paths and scalar minimization
33/36. Incomplete paths remain excluded from paired timing ratios. Among
the 33 complete pairs, the median root/MM CPU ratio is 1.010, with
interquartile range 0.976–1.053 and range 0.423–2.008. The largest relative
objective difference over commonly certified points is $6.06\times10^{-11}$.
These results support using MM as the default, while retaining the scalar-root
option. They do not imply that MM is fastest on every dataset. This study
stops at the first uncertified point and is distinct from the full-return
Figure 1 experiment.

{{< include ../analysis/outputs/scale-path-benchmark/results.qmd >}}

: Paired MM and scalar-root paths. CPU summaries use complete pairs. Unsuccessful paths remain in the counts. {#tbl-scale-paths}
